summary: Describes the VlanHello protocol that Cabletron switches use to discover their neighbors and learn the topology of a switch network. It is a vendor specification published as informational.

eli5.summary: Switches say hello to the ones next to them, so each one learns who its neighbors are and how the whole group is connected.

subtitle: Protocol for switches to discover neighbors and learn the topology of a switch fabric.

tldr.problem: Cabletron switches need to discover which switches are connected to each port and learn the overall network topology to route traffic correctly within a VLAN fabric.
tldr.mechanism: Switches send periodic Interswitch Keepalive messages out all ports. When a switch receives a keepalive from a neighbor, it records that connection, notes port state changes, and notifies topology services that build the network topology map.
tldr.outcome: The VlanHello protocol established a practical neighbor discovery mechanism for switched networks. It is a vendor-specific protocol published informally to document Cabletron's implementation.

today: RFC 2641 is a vendor specification documenting Cabletron's neighbor discovery protocol Version 4. It remains informational, describing a proprietary protocol for SFVLAN switches from the late 1990s. Modern switched networks typically use standard protocols like LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol, IEEE 802.1AB) for neighbor discovery.

sections.title: Overview of VlanHello
sections.content:
The VlanHello protocol is part of Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN (SFVLAN) product and enables switches to discover neighboring switches and establish the network topology.

The protocol is simple: at startup, each switch sends Interswitch Keepalive messages out all ports (except those preconfigured to be non-network ports). When switches hear keepalive messages from neighbors, they record the connection. If communication is lost for a predetermined time, the neighbor is removed from the topology.

As the protocol discovers network changes, it generates topology events that are delivered to local topology services. These services process events from a FIFO queue and update the switch fabric's topology tables. This architecture allows the VlanHello protocol to focus narrowly on neighbor discovery while delegating topology management to other services.
sections.eli5: Each switch periodically says hello to all its neighbors. When two switches hear each other, they know they are connected. If they stop hearing from each other, they know the connection is broken.

sections.title: Port States and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Every port on a switch can be in one of several states that indicate its role and connectivity. The VlanHello protocol manages transitions between these states based on the traffic it observes.

Unknown is the default state at initialization. When the switch receives an Interswitch Keepalive message from a neighbor, the port transitions to Network, and a "Neighbor Found" event is sent to topology services. If all neighbors leave, the port returns to Unknown or Network-Only (if the interface can only connect to other switches).

Standby ports receive but do not send keepalive messages. A port becomes Standby if the neighbor reports the local switch as Incompatible, or if the neighbor's keepalive does not include the local switch in its list (indicating one-way communication).

Access ports receive user end-station traffic. If a port receives non-keepalive traffic while Unknown, it moves to Going-To-Access for a brief period; if no keepalive arrives during this window, the port becomes Access. Network-Only ports are preconfigured for inter-switch links only.

The RFC includes a state machine diagram showing all transitions triggered by receiving keepalive messages, detecting one-way communication, and timer expiry.
sections.eli5: Ports start as Unknown. When a switch hears from a neighbor, the port becomes Network. If users plug in, the port becomes Access. The state machine keeps track of what kind of connection each port has.

sections.title: Topology Events and Timers
sections.content:
The VlanHello protocol notifies topology services of network changes through topology events. Each event describes something that happened on a port, such as a neighbor discovered (Event 1), a neighbor's features changed (Events 2-3), a neighbor timeout (Event 4), or a port down (Event 5).

Each topology event contains the event type, port number, neighbor switch identifier (MAC address plus logical port), neighbor IP and MAC addresses, functional level (software version), and a bitmap of the neighbor's capabilities. The capability bitmap includes flags for VLAN switch, link state, flood path, loop-free capability, redundancy, tap capability, uplink designation, and other features.

The RFC defines two timers. The Send Hello timer controls how often Interswitch Keepalive messages are sent (every 5 seconds in typical deployments). The Aging timer determines how long to wait before declaring a neighbor down. The Going-to-Access timer delays the transition of a port from Unknown to Access, allowing the protocol to distinguish between switch neighbors and end-station connections.
sections.eli5: When something changes—a new neighbor appears, a neighbor disappears, or a port is no longer used—the switch sends a notification. Three timers control when messages are sent, when neighbors are declared lost, and when a port becomes an access port.

sections.title: InterSwitch Message Protocol
sections.content:
VlanHello operates as part of the InterSwitch Message Protocol (ISMP), a framing protocol for switch-to-switch control messages in Cabletron's SFVLAN product. ISMP messages are encapsulated in an IEEE 802 frame with a destination multicast MAC address 01-00-1D-00-00-00 that all switches in the fabric receive.

Each ISMP packet contains a frame header, ISMP packet header, and ISMP message body. The ISMP header includes the protocol version (3.0 for VlanHello), message type (2 for keepalive), a sequence number, and an authentication code field.

The Interswitch Keepalive message (the message body of type 2) contains the sending switch's IP address, internal switch identifier, MAC address, functional level, and a bitmap of its capabilities. Most importantly, it includes a list of Base MAC entries: the MAC addresses of neighboring switches previously discovered on the same port, with each entry showing the neighbor's assigned state. This list allows receiving switches to detect if the neighbor is hearing them back (two-way communication) or if communication is one-way.
sections.eli5: Keepalive messages are like postcards sent over the network. Each one says who the switch is, what it can do, and which neighbors it hears. By reading these postcards, other switches build a map of the network.

sections.title: Topology Relay Structure
sections.content:
When VlanHello detects a topology change, it creates a topology relay structure that bundles the event information for delivery to topology services. These structures are queued in FIFO order and processed in sequence.

Each structure contains a 4-octet event type number (one of 13 defined event types), delta and current option mask fields (showing capabilities gained or lost), the port number and neighbor identifiers, neighbor chassis information, functional level, a pointer to the topology agent that generated the event, and a pointer to the next event in the queue.

Event types include Neighbor Found, Features Gained, Features Lost, Neighbor Timeout, Port Down, Neighbor Moved to Different Port, Port Reassigned, Looped Port (keepalive from self), Crossed Port (keepalive not owned by this agent), Functional Level Changed, Incompatible Protocol Version, Two-Way Communication Lost, and Sequence Number Reset (indicating a neighbor reboot).

The functional level field allows the protocol to handle backward compatibility with older SFVLAN versions, and the capability bits provide fine-grained information about each switch's features for advanced topology decisions.
sections.eli5: When the network topology changes, VlanHello creates a notification containing all the details about what changed and puts it in a queue for the topology manager to process in order.
